newsitem.title: USA: Environment strains atmosphere at G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: Environment strains atmosphere at G7 summit.

text.p: Environmental issues shaped up on Saturday as a sore point for the big industrialised states as European members criticised the United States, Canada and Japan for not supporting sharp cuts in greenhouse gases.

Ahead of a U.N. Earth Summit, the four European Union members of the rich countries' club, the Group of Seven, have had little success with their demand that the G7 aim to cut carbon dioxide and other gases by 15 percent by 2010, EU officials said.
The EU states -- Britain, France, Germany and Italy -- also ran into difficulties with their call for an international convention to protect the world's forests, they said.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, host to this year's summit, sent back the "sherpas", senior officials advising each leader, to draw up a clear statement on the environment to be issued on Sunday, they added.
German officials said Chancellor Helmut Kohl opened a frank exchange of views on the environment at a closed-door summit session and stressed the need for clear targets.
"The chancellor discussed the issue very, very openly and called it the most difficult issue at the summit," one official said. "Credible protection of the climate needs concrete reduction goals."
British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook put down North American resistence to ambitious targets to a cultural divide between Europe and the U.S. and Canada.

"Both of them find it very difficult to deal with a domestic audience which is still very much in a culture of large extravagant private cars and generous consumption of energy as a cheap commodity," he told reporters.
But the issue was alarming, he added: "The lifestyle of America and elsewhere canot be contained much beyond another quarter of a century without serious effects on our climate."
Carbon dioxide and other so-called greenhouse gases are blamed for global warming and the climate change that results.
A special U.N. General Assembly session in New York next week will discuss progress in fighting global warming since the first Earth Summit held in Rio de Janeiro five years ago.
The EU agreed last week to call for a 15 percent cut in greenhouse gases in 2010 from their 1990 levels. But the other G7 states want only a vaguer reference to reductions without any precise target.

The G7 comprises the United States, Japan, Germany, Britain, France, Italy and Canada, and their leaders were joined at this year's annual summit by Russian President Boris Yeltsin for nearly all their talks.
The annual summits often set the tone for coordinated policy work over the next year.

In contrast to greenhouse gases, the U.S. has been pressing its G7 partners to agree to link export credit guarantees to a recipient country's record in protecting the environment. Washington refused credits for China's Three Gorges Dam project because it did not meet ecological standards.
German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said Bonn opposed this linkage and a group of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development would be asked to study the issue.

In his speech, Kohl quoted a German parliament report on greenhouse gases showing that the United States accounted for 24.25 percent of the world's carbon emissions -- by far the highest level in the world and rising between 1990 and 1994.
China came next at 13.3 percent and rising in the same period, then came Russia and the former Soviet republics with 11.7 percent and falling and Asia without China at 9.6 percent and rising.
Japan accounted for 5.37 percent of the world's greenhouse gases, with the total on the rise, and Germany was responsible for 4.17 percent and its share was falling.
